cards.explanation: The answer is that their god delivered Samson into their hands. The lords rejoice and say, "Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hands." They are praising Dagon, their god, for putting Samson in their hands. I think the whole room felt like they'd won the big game.

The answer is True. When the people see Samson, they praise their god for delivering "…our enemy who destroyed our land and multiplied our dead." Those are their words about Samson, and they're loud about it. I think a crowd that's been holding that in for a while finally gets to let it out.
The word is entertain. The Philistines say, "Call for Samson to entertain us." So out of the prison he comes. I think a crowd with merry hearts wanted a show, and he was who they asked for.
The word is pillars. The text says, "And they stationed him between the pillars." Remember that word, friends, because those pillars are about to matter a lot.

The answer is that Samson wants to lean against the pillars. He tells the servant, "Lead me where I can feel the pillars supporting the temple, so I can lean against them." The servant is holding his hand, so he's being led. I bet it sounded like an ordinary request to the servant.
The answer is True. Samson prays, "Strengthen me, O God, just once more…" He asks God directly, and he asks for it one time. Notice he starts with "…please remember me." so he comes to God first.

The answer is that he wants to pay back the Philistines. Samson asks that "…with one vengeful blow I may pay back the Philistines for my two eyes." He says it plainly to the LORD. I think this is a heavy moment, so I'll just say it's what he asked.

The answer is "Let me die with the Philistines." With his right hand on one pillar and his left on the other, Samson says those words. I think this is the heaviest line in the passage, so we'll let it stand as it is.

The answer is that the temple falls on the lords and all the people. Samson pushes "…with all his might, and the temple fell on the lords and all the people in it." The two pillars he had his hands on were holding it up. One more thing to notice, friends: it's a heavy ending to the scene.
The answer is False. The text says, "So in his death he killed more than he had killed in his life." More in that one moment than all the years before it. That's what the writer tells us.

The answer is his father Manoah's tomb. His brothers and his father's family carried him back and buried him "…between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah." His family came for him. I think that's a quiet, kind ending to a loud story.
